title: Ivo and Nyx's Loop of Lights
markdown:
Dawn arrived as a splash of gold on the workshop roof. Colours woke up all at once. Ivo the tiny mechanic bounced out of bed with his goggles already on, as if night had been a brief interruption in a longer experiment. Today was the day.

“Nyx! Grandad Sol!” His voice was a tiny burst barely contained. “The dance-light machine! It’s ready to perform its spectacular light show!”

Nyx the raven came through the window, midnight feathers catching the new sun. She bobbed her head. She liked Ivo’s inventions, especially the ones that painted air.

They dashed — tiny boots, black wings — into the workshop, a delightful jumble packed to the rafters with blinking bulbs, gears that whispered, and a magnificent towering contraption of polished brass and gleaming crystal that Ivo had named, with love and a slightly too-long label, the Spectacular Lumina Dancer. Ivo’s heart did a proud thump.

“Just a few final tweaks, and it’ll be absolutely spectacular.”

The tweaks did not help. The lights flickered, a weak kiss on the walls, nothing like the show they had imagined. He tightened screws. He polished lenses. Nyx tapped the cool brass, then pecked a wire with the care of someone testing a frozen puddle. The machine coughed dimly. Ivo’s chest went heavy. He did not name the feeling. The dimness named it for him.

Grandad Sol’s footsteps were gentle on the boards. Silver hair, kind eyes, a rumble that made the workshop feel less accused.

“Now, Ivo. This dance-light machine. How do those colours pop?”

Ivo frowned at the tangle. “I connected this wire for blue, then this for green, then this for red. Then I had to do it again. Blue, green, red. Over and over. Like the clockwork bird last spring.”

Grandad Sol nodded. “What if you could tell it to do all of those colours again and again without connecting each wire every single time?”

“But how?”

Nyx had been hopping the floor. She pecked a smooth grey stone and nudged it to Ivo. Then another, identical. Then another. The pile grew: one, then one, then one, a line with a rhythm.

Ivo watched the beak, the stones, the repeat.

“The stones,” he gasped. “The repeating action. A loop. One instruction to do a whole set of things again.”

He scrambled to the panel. “Not blue, then green, then red, then blue again, then green again. Do blue, green, red. Then repeat that whole sequence.”

His fingers found the little brass dial Grandad had given him weeks ago, a tiny arrow etched on its face. Blue: this. Green: this. Red: this. He turned the arrow.

“For the whole dance: repeat.”

He pressed the main button. The air crackled, smelling of warm brass and ozone. Sapphire, emerald, and ruby leapt up the walls, across the ceiling, over the floor, pulsed, spun, found one another and did it again, and again, without Ivo’s hands flying back to every wire. It was the show they had imagined, and then a little more, because the loop did not get tired or forget the green. Nyx cawed and saluted with both wings.

Grandad Sol’s smile reached his eyes. He did not give a lecture about birds and toasters. He named the dial’s trick, because a good name keeps in a pocket.

“Loops. Repeating instructions. Your clockwork bird’s legs already knew. Nyx’s stones knew. Now the lights know.”

Ivo grinned at the still-dancing colours. In his head a clockwork band struck up, then sat down again; there would be time. He left the Lumina Dancer looping its three honest colours, a small aurora that did not get tired. Nyx added one more stone to the line on the floor, as if to keep the idea from rolling away. Grandad poured tea. The arrow on the dial held. The lights, having been told once, kept their promise until the sun was properly up, which in a workshop is the only review that matters.
